title: Masks and counting bits
sub: Number of 1 Bits, Power of Two and Hamming distance: Kernighan’s trick, Unity layer masks and the built-in popcount
cards/0/body:
An int in C# is 32 bits, and bit k is worth 2ᵏ: 52 = 110100₂ = 32 + 16 + 4. In hexadecimal one digit is exactly 4 bits: 0x34 = 0011 0100 = 52, and 0xFF is eight ones.

Six operators: & (AND: 1 where both are 1), | (OR), ^ (exclusive OR: 1 where the bits differ), ~ (flips all 32 bits), << k (shift left: multiply by 2ᵏ, bits pushed past bit 31 are lost) and >> k (shift right).

A mask is a number with 1s in the positions you care about. With bit k you do four things: test (x >> k) & 1, set x | (1 << k), clear x & ~(1 << k), toggle x ^ (1 << k). A mask is also a set of up to 32 elements: union is |, intersection is &, “nothing in common” is (a & b) == 0. The k lowest 1s are (1 << k) − 1. The letters of a word are a 26-bit mask m |= 1 << (c - 'a'); all subsets of n elements are the numbers 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.

Sign. Negative numbers are stored in two’s complement: bit 31 is worth −2³¹. So −1 is all 32 ones, int.MinValue has a 1 only in bit 31, and ~x == −x − 1. The >> shift on an int copies the sign bit (−8 >> 1 = −4); on a uint it shifts in zeros. When you want “just 32 bits” with no sign, use uint.
cards/0/code:
int x = 52;                       // 0b_0011_0100 = 0x34
bool has2 = ((x >> 2) & 1) != 0;  // true: bit 2 is set
x |= 1 << 0;                      // 53: set bit 0
x &= ~(1 << 4);                   // 37: cleared bit 4
x ^= 1 << 5;                      // 5: toggled bit 5
int all = -1;                     // 0xFFFFFFFF: all 32 ones
uint top = 0x80000000;            // bit 31 only; as an int this is int.MinValue

for (int mask = 0; mask < 1 << 3; mask++) { }   // 8 subsets of 3 elements: 000 … 111
cards/1/body:
The most common place for bits in Unity is layers. gameObject.layer is the layer index, 0 to 31, while a LayerMask is a 32-bit mask: bit k is set if layer k is included. Physics takes the mask: Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, dist, mask) only hits the included layers.

The classic mistake is passing an index instead of a mask. Raycast(…, 8) is the mask 0b1000, which is layer 3, not layer 8. The mask for layer 8 is 1 << 8. By name: LayerMask.GetMask("Enemy", "Ground") returns a mask, while LayerMask.NameToLayer("Enemy") returns an index that you still have to shift into a mask. “Every layer except” is ~mask. Whether an object is in a mask: (mask & (1 << go.layer)) != 0.

Flags. A [Flags] enum is the same mask with names: values are powers of two, you combine them with | and test with &. On .NET Core 2.1+ the JIT turns HasFlag into that same test with no allocation, but in Unity you should not count on it: the call may box the enum. In hot code write (s & X) != 0.
cards/2/q: In the project the Enemy layer has index 8. The raycast must hit enemies only. Which call is right?
cards/2/explain: The last parameter is a mask, not an index. The mask for layer 8 is a 1 in bit 8, that is 1 << 8 = 256. LayerMask.GetMask("Enemy") gives the same value.
cards/2/wrong/0: 8 = 0b1000 is the mask for layer 3. The raycast hits layer 3 and never sees the enemies.
cards/2/wrong/2: ~8 is every bit except bit 3: almost every layer except layer 3.
cards/2/wrong/3: NameToLayer returns the index 8 — the same mistake as the first option. You need 1 << LayerMask.NameToLayer("Enemy").
cards/3/title: Number of 1 Bits: the problem and the brute-force loop
cards/3/body:
Number of 1 Bits (LeetCode #191): how many 1s are in the binary form of a 32-bit number. This is the Hamming weight, or popcount. Example: 52 = 110100₂ → 3. If the number comes in as an int, convert it to uint right away: you care about the bits, not the sign.

Brute force checks all 32 bits: add the lowest bit and shift right. That is O(32) = O(1), and the interviewer will immediately ask: can you take as many steps as there are 1s? For sparse masks — flags, layers, 1–3 ones out of 32 — that is ten times less work.

Why uint and not int: with while (x != 0) the loop never ends on a negative int — >> copies the sign bit, and −1 >> 1 is −1 again.
cards/4/body:
Subtracting 1 borrows from the lowest 1: it becomes 0, every 0 below it becomes 1, and the bits above do not change. 52 = 110100, 51 = 110011. In n & (n − 1) the bits above that position agree and survive, while from it downwards they are opposite and cancel. The result: exactly the lowest 1 is cleared, 52 → 48.

Invariant: each turn of the loop removes one 1, so there are exactly popcount(n) turns. Time O(k), where k is the number of 1s; memory O(1).

Power of Two (#231) is a number with a single 1: one Kernighan step gives 0. The test is n > 0 && (n & (n − 1)) == 0. The n > 0 part is required: zero has no 1s at all, and int.MinValue also has a single 1 — the sign bit 31 — so the bit test alone would call it a power of two.
cards/5/q: Build a popcount that runs once per 1 bit, and the power-of-two test.
cards/5/explain: The (uint)n cast keeps the bits and drops the sign; without it, uint x = n does not compile. x &= x − 1 clears the lowest 1 — one turn per 1 bit. For the power of two, n > 0 rules out zero and every negative number, int.MinValue included.
cards/6/task: Step through the trace on n = 52 = 110100₂: each step is n − 1 first, then n & (n − 1). The rig stops twice and asks what the next step gives.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: The subtraction borrows from the lowest 1, bit 4: it goes out, the four 0s below it turn into 1s, and bit 5 stays. 110000 − 1 = 101111 = 47. The 32 = 100000 is n & (n − 1) — that comes on the next step.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: count = 2, n = 32 = 100000₂, n − 1 = 011111₂. What does n &= n − 1 do?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: 32 has a single 1, and all six bits of 32 and 31 are opposite, so the AND gives 0. count = 3: exactly as many steps as 52 has 1s, not 32.
cards/7/q: This IsPowerOfTwo returns true for n = int.MinValue. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/7/explain: int.MinValue has a 1 only in bit 31. n − 1 wraps around to int.MaxValue = 0x7FFFFFFF — no 1s in common, the AND gives 0, and the bit test passes. A negative number is not a power of two, so rule out every n <= 0: if (n <= 0) return false.
cards/8/body:
Hamming Distance (#461): in how many positions the bits of x and y differ. Minimum Bit Flips to Convert Number (#2220): how many bits of start to flip to get goal. It is one problem: the differing bits are exactly the 1s of x ^ y, and each of them is flipped once. The answer is popcount(x ^ y).

Built-in popcount. .NET Core 3.0+ has BitOperations.PopCount in System.Numerics: when the CPU supports it (POPCNT on x86, its counterpart on ARM64) this is a single instruction. .NET 7+ also has int.PopCount. Unity has no BitOperations — its profile is .NET Standard 2.1. There, use math.countbits from Unity.Mathematics (under Burst it also becomes an instruction) or the Kernighan loop. For powers of two Unity has Mathf.IsPowerOfTwo, and .NET 6+ has BitOperations.IsPow2.

In an interview, write and explain the loop first, then say that in production you would use the built-in popcount — that is the senior answer.
cards/9/q: Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: The Hamming distance between 1 (0001₂) and 4 (0100₂) is 2
cards/9/options/1: If x & (x − 1) == 0, then x is a power of two
cards/9/options/2: The Kernighan loop takes 32 steps on uint.MaxValue
cards/9/options/3: BitOperations.PopCount can be called from a Unity script
cards/9/options/4: (mask & (1 << go.layer)) != 0 means the object is on one of the mask’s layers
cards/9/explain: 1 ^ 4 = 0101₂ — two 1s. x & (x − 1) == 0 holds for zero and for int.MinValue too, so you also need x > 0. uint.MaxValue has 32 ones — one step each. BitOperations arrived in .NET Core 3.0, while Unity compiles against .NET Standard 2.1, where you use math.countbits. The last option tests bit number go.layer of the mask.
cards/10/q: You are solving Number of 1 Bits out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: is the number 32-bit, signed or not, how often is it called
cards/10/items/1: Brute force: check all 32 bits with a shift — O(32)
cards/10/items/2: Idea: n & (n − 1) clears the lowest 1 — one step per 1 bit
cards/10/items/3: Code on a uint so that the sign-copying shift does not get in the way
cards/10/items/5: Complexity: O(k) in the number of 1s, O(1) memory
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: 0, uint.MaxValue, a negative int; in production, the built-in popcount
cards/10/explain: The problem, the baseline, the idea, the code, a check on an example, complexity and edge cases. Mentioning BitOperations.PopCount and math.countbits at the end shows you know how real code does it.
cards/11/body:
The Kernighan loop is good when there are few 1s. Without a loop or branches, SWAR — “SIMD within a register” — counts them: add neighbouring bits in pairs, pairs into nibbles, nibbles into bytes, and a single multiplication collects the bytes. 12 operations for any number, independent of the data.

This is exactly how the built-in popcount falls back when there is no POPCNT instruction. Nobody expects the code by heart in an interview, but explaining the idea of “parallel sums in bit fields” is a plus.
cards/11/deep:
Why the multiplication adds the bytes. 0x01010101 = 2⁰ + 2⁸ + 2¹⁶ + 2²⁴, so x * 0x01010101 is the sum of x shifted by 0, 8, 16 and 24 bits. The top byte ends up holding the sum of all four bytes of x. Each byte is ≤ 8 and the sum is ≤ 32, so nothing carries between bytes.

A table. Another way is an array of 256 precomputed answers and four lookups by byte. In a hot loop it loses to SWAR and POPCNT: memory accesses and cache misses.

.NET. BitOperations.PopCount(uint) and PopCount(ulong) are intrinsics: the JIT emits POPCNT (on x86 with POPCNT support) or a vector instruction on ARM64, and falls back to a SWAR-style software version otherwise. On x86 you can check with System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.Popcnt.IsSupported.

Unity. math.countbits exists for int, uint, long, ulong and the vector types. In Burst code the compiler emits the instruction when the target supports it; outside Burst it is plain C# — the same SWAR arithmetic. Next to it are math.tzcnt and math.lzcnt (trailing and leading zeros); they come up in the bitboards lesson.
